inventory.name: Local Network Access permission check for WebSocket connections: connections from public secure pages to loopback, RFC 1918 private, or link-local targets require a user permission grant; denial (or a non-secure initiating page) blocks the connection (Chrome/Edge 147)

loopback-network permission delegation: WebSocket connections from iframe content to local addresses proceed only when the iframe carries allow="loopback-network" (the same delegation is referenced for Isolated Web App manifests)

Chrome enterprise policies for the restriction: LocalNetworkAccessAllowedForUrls (per-origin allow without prompt), LocalNetworkAccessBlockedForUrls (per-origin block), LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut (enterprise-wide temporary opt-out during rollout) — confirmed verbatim by the ChromeStatus record as the applying policy set

syntax.rationale: The restriction adds no grammar of its own; the declarable surface it gates is the WebSocket constructor call into a local address — new WebSocket("ws://127.0.0.1:8787/bridge") — shown in the page's <pre><code> block with its open/error listeners. That connection form is the syntax of record.

inputs.rationale: The trigger set is the target address family: loopback (127.0.0.1, localhost, ::1), RFC 1918 private (10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x), link-local (169.254.x, fe80::/10) — enumerated with examples in the address-range table.

outputs.rationale: The observable outcomes are stated: the browser shows the Local Network Access permission prompt, and on denial the WebSocket connection is blocked.

errors.rationale: The documented failure mode is the blocked connection — the user denies the prompt, or no prompt is shown because the site is not secure. The example block registers the WebSocket error event ("Local WebSocket blocked.") as the page-side signal; no dedicated exception surface is documented.

context.rationale: The conditions under which the check runs and passes: HTTPS secure context, iframe delegation via allow="loopback-network", and the user's permission grant.

lifecycle.rationale: Shipped in Chrome 147 and Edge 147 (desktop, Android), enabled by default, with flag chrome://flags/#local-network-access-check-websockets and a temporary enterprise opt-out during rollout.

examples.rationale: The page's <pre><code> block connects a public HTTPS page to a companion app on ws://127.0.0.1:8787/bridge and logs the error path — the exact flow the permission gates.

compatibility.rationale: Support table: Chrome 147+ and Edge 147+ enabled by default (desktop, Android); Firefox and Safari listed with no position.

securityPrivacy.rationale: The page documents the threat model the feature exists to close: silent cross-origin WebSocket access to unauthenticated private-network devices (routers, printers, dev servers) from public sites; the prompt makes that reachability user-visible and deniable.

syntax.rationale: Disclosed edge case: the complete declaration form is the iframe attribute value allow="loopback-network", documented in the requirements list as inline code. The page's single <pre><code> block demonstrates the gated WebSocket call rather than an iframe, so this dimension rests on the in-context attribute form — no grammar has been invented or decorated beyond it.

inputs.rationale: The delegation input is the presence of allow="loopback-network" on the iframe whose content initiates the local WebSocket connection.

outputs.rationale: With delegation and a granted prompt the connection proceeds; the page's what-changes section states the prompt/deny outcome for the connection the iframe initiates.

errors.rationale: Without the required delegation the iframe's local WebSocket falls under the default failure mode: the connection is blocked when permission is not granted.

context.rationale: The mitigation section documents the other contexts of the same attribute — Isolated Web Apps can use allow="loopback-network" in the manifest, and pages served from http://localhost are themselves a local context under different rules than public pages.

lifecycle.rationale: The delegation requirement ships with the same Chrome/Edge 147 rollout, enabled-by-default status, and feature flag as the restriction it scopes.

examples.rationale: The page carries one <pre><code> block — the gated loopback WebSocket connection this delegation authorizes for embedded content; the iframe usage itself appears in the requirements list rather than in the code example.

compatibility.rationale: Delegation is part of the Chromium-only rollout (Chrome/Edge 147+); Firefox and Safari have no position on the underlying Local Network Access work.

securityPrivacy.rationale: The delegation bounds which embedded content may reach the user's private network at all — it is one of the security controls that closes the silent cross-origin access described in the page's threat model.

syntax.rationale: Disclosed edge case: the declarable surface is the three policy-name keys — LocalNetworkAccessAllowedForUrls, LocalNetworkAccessBlockedForUrls, LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut — documented as inline code in the policy table. The page carries no <pre><code> grammar for admin policy configuration and none has been invented here; the schema forces this dimension to documented.

inputs.rationale: Each policy's input shape is stated in the table: origin lists for the allow/block policies, and an enterprise-wide toggle for the temporary opt-out.

outputs.rationale: The documented effects: allowed origins connect without a prompt, blocked origins are barred from local-network connections, and the opt-out disables the restriction enterprise-wide during rollout.

errors.rationale: Absent an enterprise exemption, the default failure mode from what-changes applies: a denied or unprompted (non-secure) local WebSocket connection is blocked.

context.rationale: The policies are Chrome enterprise deployment controls; the ChromeStatus record notes enterprise notification from milestone 141, ahead of the 147 ship.

lifecycle.rationale: LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut is explicitly a rollout-period mechanism; the same at-a-glance table records the flag and enabled-by-default state of the restriction it tempers.

examples.rationale: The page's single <pre><code> block illustrates the gated loopback connection these policies exempt; no policy-configuration example exists on the page and none has been added.

compatibility.rationale: Enterprise policies are Chromium mechanisms riding the Chrome/Edge 147 rollout; the browser-support table records no position for Firefox or Safari.

securityPrivacy.rationale: The policies are themselves the security control surface: enterprise administrators scope which origins may reach the private network, and whether the per-user permission prompt is bypassed entirely.
